hook.text: On a hundred items, almost any code is fast. The interview question is what it costs at a million, and which structure keeps it cheap.

plan.text: Thirty-five questions, argued with counts, not code: eight with a figure each, three inside those, and twenty-four quickly.

big.text: Question one. What is Big-O notation, and why do interviewers care? It says how time or memory grows with the input size, n, ignoring constants.

big-count.text: A double loop over a hundred items checks under five thousand pairs. Instant.

big-million.text: At a million items, it's half a trillion.

big-model.text: Model it at a hundred million checks a second, an assumption: about eighty-three minutes. One pass over the million: a hundredth of a second.

big-why.text: That's why they care: Big-O predicts whether a solution survives its real input. The usual game is turning a brute-force n squared into n.

big-next.text: But constants are dropped, so at a hundred items the brute force is often fine, and simpler. Say what it costs, and where it stops being fine.

hash.text: Question two. When do you reach for a hash map? When you need lookups and inserts by key in constant time on average: counting, grouping, have I seen this?

hash-twosum.text: It turns Two Sum's double loop into one pass: at each number, ask the map for target minus it, then store the number. Linear time, at the cost of linear memory.

hash-collide.text: Average is the key word. With a thousand buckets, a shared bucket is more likely than not by the thirty-eighth key.

hash-worst.text: The follow-up is the worst case. Give a thousand keys the same hash, and filling a Python set takes nearly six hundred thousand key comparisons. With distinct hashes, none.

hash-set.text: That's a hash set: constant on average, linear space, and linear per operation at worst.

amort.text: Question three. What is amortized O of one, and when does it apply? It spreads a rare expensive step's cost over the cheap ones around it.

amort-run.text: Append a million items to a Python list. It runs out of room eighty-six times, and each move to a bigger block can copy every item so far.

amort-total.text: Add those copies up: about eight copies per append, at any length. Constant, on average.

amort-factor.text: A textbook array doubles, for under two copies an append. Python grows by about an eighth, so it copies more often. Any fixed factor keeps it constant, a hash table's rehash too.

amort-spike.text: But that's an average, not a promise per call: the append that triggers the last resize can copy nine hundred thirty-nine thousand items. On a latency budget, allocate up front.

stack.text: Question four. When is a stack the right structure? When the problem is about the most recent thing still open: nesting, undo, backtracking. Last in, first out.

stack-count.text: A counter can't do it. This string opens and closes one round and one square bracket, so counting accepts it. But the round one closes while the square one inside is open.

stack-run.text: A stack keeps the openers, newest on top, and each closer must match the top: rejected.

stack-queue.text: A queue matches the oldest opener instead, so it gets both wrong: it accepts this one, and rejects a correctly nested string.

stack-next.text: Depth-first search is the same idea: the path you're on is the stack.
